young.html: Socrates meets a brilliant teenager named Theaetetus, who is very good at math. Socrates asks him a question that sounds easy: What is knowledge? Not “what do you know?” but what is knowing?

Socrates says he is like a midwife, a helper at births, as his mother was. He doesn't have ideas of his own to give; he helps other people bring their ideas into the world, and then checks whether each idea is healthy or not.

Theaetetus tries three answers. First: knowing is seeing and feeling things. But if you hear a language you don't speak, you hear the sounds without knowing what they mean. Second: knowing is believing something true. But a lucky guess can be true! Third: knowing is a true belief plus a reason. But what kind of reason? They can't agree. The book ends without an answer, and Socrates says that's fine: at least Theaetetus now knows what he doesn't know.
Along the way Socrates compares memory to a wax tablet, like the ones Greek children wrote on. Experiences press into the wax like a seal. Good wax keeps the marks clear. Soft wax smudges them.

young.name: gb-wax-tablet
young.cap: Choose a kind of wax and stamp some memories. Then let the days pass.

young.html: Wax memory test. Press a coin or a key firmly into a lump of clay or playdough, and gently into another. Leave them for a day. Which print is clearer? Now try the memory version: one person reads a list of ten words once, quickly; another reads it slowly three times. Who remembers more tomorrow?

full.html: This rung covers four of Plato's later dialogues about knowledge, language and being: the Theaetetus (about 369 BC), the Sophist, the Cratylus and the Parmenides. The Theaetetus is the place to start.

Theaetetus was a real person, a gifted Athenian mathematician who did important early work on irrational lengths and on the regular solids, and who died young after a battle. In the dialogue he is a teenager, said to look a lot like Socrates (snub nose and all), and the pupil of the geometer Theodorus. He tells Socrates how Theodorus showed that the square roots of 3, 5 and so on up to 17 cannot be measured by any whole unit, and how he and a friend then sorted all numbers into “square” and “oblong” kinds.

full.title: Theaetetus' square and oblong numbers
full.q: Theaetetus calls a number “square” if it is a whole number times itself (like $9 = 3 \times 3$) and “oblong” otherwise. Sort 12, 16 and 17, and say which have whole-number square roots.
steps: $12 = 3 \times 4$ (or $2 \times 6$), never a number times itself: oblong.
Only square numbers have whole-number roots. Theodorus had shown that the roots of oblong numbers like 3, 5 and 17 are not even fractions: they are irrational.

full.html: Socrates says his mother was a midwife and he practices the same art on minds: he cannot give birth to wisdom himself, but helps young men deliver their ideas and tests whether each is real or a “wind-egg.” Theaetetus says he is amazed and dizzy at the puzzles. Socrates answers:

full.text: I see, my dear Theaetetus, that Theodorus had a true insight into your nature when he said that you were a philosopher, for wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. IV, Clarendon Press

head: Answer
Where it comes from
The trouble
rows: Linked to Protagoras's saying, “Man is the measure of all things,” and to Heraclitus's view that everything is always changing
If each person's perception is true for him, no one is wiser than anyone else, and Protagoras could teach nothing. And we hear foreign speech without knowing what it means.
Then how is false judgment possible? And a jury persuaded of the truth by a clever speaker has true judgment but not knowledge.
A theory Socrates says he heard “in a dream”
Every meaning they find for “account” either adds nothing or already assumes knowledge.
full.cap: The three definitions, in our own words.

full.html: To explain false judgment, Socrates tries two models of the mind. The first is the wax tablet:

full.text: I would have you imagine, then, that there exists in the mind of man a block of wax, which is of different sizes in different men; harder, moister, and having more or less of purity in one than another, and in some of an intermediate quality.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. IV, Clarendon Press

full.name: gb-wax-tablet
full.cap: Socrates' kinds of wax, in our simplified model. Stamp impressions, then let time pass.

full.html: A mistake, on this model, is fitting a new sight to the wrong old imprint, like putting a foot into the wrong shoe. But that cannot explain mistakes in pure thought, such as thinking 7 + 5 is 11. So Socrates tries a second model: the mind as an aviary of birds, each bird a piece of knowledge. You can own a bird without holding it, and grab the wrong one. That fails too.

An open ending. The Theaetetus ends without a definition. Socrates says that Theaetetus will now be gentler and wiser, “not fancying that you know what you do not know.” Then he leaves to answer the charges against him, the same day as the Euthyphro.

Thinking an open ending means the dialogue failed. Each refuted answer teaches something: knowledge is more than seeing, more than being right, and more than right plus words. Philosophers still discuss the third answer, often stated as “justified true belief.”

items: Sophist: a visitor from Elea, called the Stranger, defines the sophist by repeatedly dividing kinds into two, as one might sort fishing into kinds until reaching angling. To say the sophist deals in falsehood, he must explain how one can speak of what is not. His answer: “not being” means being different from something.

Cratylus: are names right by nature or by agreement? Hermogenes says by agreement; Cratylus says by nature. Socrates offers many playful word origins, then says we should learn about things from the things themselves, not from their names.
Parmenides: a young Socrates meets the old philosopher Parmenides and his student Zeno, who raise hard objections to the theory of Forms. Plato shows his own theory being tested.

deep.html: “What is knowledge?” is the central question of the part of philosophy called epistemology. In 1963 the philosopher Edmund Gettier published a three-page paper with cases where someone has a justified true belief by luck, and it seemed not to be knowledge. Discussions of his cases look back to the Theaetetus's third answer.

Aristotle, next on this ladder, gave his own account of scientific knowledge in the Posterior Analytics, as knowing the cause through a demonstration. Descartes, much later, began his search for certain knowledge by doubting the senses, much as Socrates did with the first answer.

items: What is the difference between knowing something and just believing it?
Is there anything you are completely sure of? How do you know?
Protagoras said each person is the measure of what is true for him. When is that right (“this soup is too hot for me”) and when is it wrong?

questions: What is something you know for sure? How did you come to know it?
Can you be right without knowing? Think of a lucky guess on a test.
Socrates said he was a midwife for ideas. Who helps you think through your ideas?
Is your memory more like hard wax or soft wax? Does it depend on the subject?
Philosophy begins in wonder, Socrates says. What do you wonder about?
Is it all right for a book or a conversation to end without an answer?
